newsitem.title: USA: Fed may up rates, but Greenspan is key--Fed alumni.
newsitem.headline: Fed may up rates, but Greenspan is key--Fed alumni.

text.p: The economy is healthy, labour markets are tight, consumer spending is showing incipient signs of waning and inflation remains a missing person; you are dazed with mixed signals but still have to decide on whether to raise interest rates.
So who are you going to call?
Alan Greenspan, the Chairman of the Federal Reserve.

As economists inside and outside the Fed grapple with a mixed bag of economic data ahead of the bank's policy-setting meeting on May 20, the decision whether to alter monetary policy again weighs heavily on the mind of one man.

Although deciphering Greenspan's encrypted messages is no easy task, several experienced former Fed officials and sources close to the central bank said there are some signs that indicate the Fed may opt to raise rates on Tuesday.

Analysts said recent data suggest the economy might be losing steam after seven consecutive years of firm growth, giving the Fed room to take a wait-and-see attitude and leave rates unchanged on Tuesday.

But pressure from interest rate hawks sitting at the Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee combined with the Fed's highly publicised commitment to preemptive policy might be enough reason to raise the federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point to 5.75 percent. The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for short term loans.
At its last meeting on March 25, the Fed raised rates for the first time in more than two years, bumping them up a quarter percentage point to 5.5 percent.

"If added up, all the recent statistical leading indicators are more, 'Don't do it' than, 'Do it.' But I think the Fed is looking at 1998; they are still concerned about how rapidly the economy is still growing," said former Fed Vice Chairman Preston Martin.
Martin said he believes the Fed will decide to increase the funds rate by a quarter point on Tuesday. But he added that the final decision will once again be in Greenspan's hands.

"It's going to be a very split vote, and since it's going to be a divided audience, Greenspan could probably hold it off if he wanted to," said Martin, who is currently the chairman of San Francisco-based HomeVest Financial Services Inc.
Pundits said the Fed still appeared to be very sceptical that the 4.9 percent unemployment rate seen in April could be sustained without fuelling inflation.
"The signals that they're looking at have been very mixed," said William Ford, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.

"The Fed is less certain, but still, given the cautious nature of the policy and strong bias that the chairman has to head off inflation, it's still likely they will give one more uptick to interest rates," he added.

Ford, who holds the Banking Chair at Middle Tennessee State University and works as a senior economic advisor for TeleCheck Services Inc., said odds call for another quarter point increase in the funds rate on May 20.
Despite recent criticism from some Washington lawmakers, experts said Greenspan still has enough leeway on Capitol Hill and at the White House to raise rates once more.

"Greenspan is concerned about his popularity because he's certainly thinking about one more appointment as chairman, and that is less than two years away now," said a source close to the Fed who asked not to be identified.

"But I think the conditioning factor in that is Greenspan's close relationship with Secretary (of the Treasury Robert) Rubin. The Fed decision will also depend on the signals that Rubin is giving the Chairman," the source said.
Rubin said on Thursday that he thinks it is too early to say the U.S. economy has entered a new era, adding that there was a need to watch for inflation.
"I've always remained very watchful and very sceptical about the notion that somehow ... we're in a new era of wonderful conditions with respect to inflation," Rubin said.
